summary.title: Tumor PD-L1 selectively suppresses type I interferon in myeloid cells to suppress CTL recruitment to promote lung metastasis
summary.authors: John D Klement; Priscilla S Redd; Chunwan Lu; Alyssa D Merting; Dakota B Poschel; Dafeng Yang; Gang Zhou; David H Munn; Kebin Liu
summary.executive_summary: This study redefines the mechanism of PD-L1 mediated immune suppression in the context of lung metastasis. While PD-L1 on tumor cells is known to inhibit T cells directly, this paper demonstrates that in the absence of other microenvironmental factors, tumor PD-L1 does not directly suppress cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) function. Instead, the authors found that tumor PD-L1 acts on myeloid cells expressing PD-1 (mPD-1). This interaction suppresses type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling and STAT1 activation within myeloid cells. Consequently, the expression of chemokines Cxcl9 and Cxcl10, which are critical for recruiting CTLs to the lung, is repressed. The study utilized murine models of triple-negative breast cancer (4T1) and colorectal cancer (CT26), employing CRISPR-mediated knockout of PD-L1, single-cell RNA sequencing, and myeloid cell depletion. Results showed that while primary tumor growth was unaffected by PD-L1 loss, lung metastasis was significantly reduced in a CTL-dependent manner. Depleting myeloid cells abolished the metastatic advantage conferred by PD-L1. Human patient data correlated response to PD-1 blockade with IFN-I responses in myeloid cells. The core finding is the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis, which controls CTL infiltration into lung metastases, suggesting that targeting this axis or enhancing IFN-I signaling could improve immunotherapy outcomes for metastatic disease.

Executive Summary
This study redefines the mechanism of PD-L1 mediated immune suppression in the context of lung metastasis. While PD-L1 on tumor cells is known to inhibit T cells directly, this paper demonstrates that in the absence of other microenvironmental factors, tumor PD-L1 does not directly suppress cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) function. Instead, the authors found that tumor PD-L1 acts on myeloid cells expressing PD-1 (mPD-1). This interaction suppresses type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling and STAT1 activation within myeloid cells. Consequently, the expression of chemokines Cxcl9 and Cxcl10, which are critical for recruiting CTLs to the lung, is repressed. The study utilized murine models of triple-negative breast cancer (4T1) and colorectal cancer (CT26), employing CRISPR-mediated knockout of PD-L1, single-cell RNA sequencing, and myeloid cell depletion. Results showed that while primary tumor growth was unaffected by PD-L1 loss, lung metastasis was significantly reduced in a CTL-dependent manner. Depleting myeloid cells abolished the metastatic advantage conferred by PD-L1. Human patient data correlated response to PD-1 blockade with IFN-I responses in myeloid cells. The core finding is the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis, which controls CTL infiltration into lung metastases, suggesting that targeting this axis or enhancing IFN-I signaling could improve immunotherapy outcomes for metastatic disease.

Research Context
PD-L1/PD-1 blockade is a standard therapy but its mechanism in metastasis is unclear. Prior theories suggest tumor PD-L1 directly shields cells from T cell killing. However, clinical data shows metastasis is the dominant cause of mortality. Recent data indicates PD-1 expression exists on non-T cell populations like myeloid cells. The specific link between tumor PD-L1, myeloid PD-1, and metastasis remains unknown.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Does tumor PD-L1 directly inhibit CTL function in a simplified microenvironment? Does tumor PD-L1 promote metastasis independent of primary tumor growth? Is there an intermediate cell type mediating the effect of tumor PD-L1 on CTLs? Does tumor PD-L1 engage myeloid PD-1 to suppress type I interferon signaling? Does this suppression of interferon signaling impair chemokine production and CTL recruitment?

Methodological Details
Two murine cancer models were used: 4T1 triple-negative breast cancer and CT26 colorectal cancer. PD-L1 was knocked out using CRISPR technology in HEK293FT cells to generate lentivirus. Tumor cells were transduced with lentivirus and selected with puromycin. In vitro cytotoxicity assays used a tumor-specific CTL line (2/20) against 4T1 and CT26. In vivo models included orthotopic injection for primary tumors and tail vein injection for metastasis. Lung metastasis was quantified by inflating lungs with India ink and counting nodules. Myeloid cells were depleted using clodronate liposomes in tumor-bearing mice. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on CD45+ leukocytes from colonized lungs. Flow cytometry was used to analyze surface markers and intracellular signaling in lung cells. Human relevance was assessed using TCGA datasets and melanoma cohort data.

Procedures And Architectures
CRISPR/Cas9 was used to generate PD-L1 deficient (KO) tumor cell lines. The 2/20 CTL line recognizes the H2-L d -restricted AH1 epitope of gp70. RNA sequencing involved aligning reads to mm10 reference genome using STARv2.5. Single-cell libraries were generated using Chromium Single Cell 3' Reagent Kit v3. Data analysis utilized Seurat for clustering and DoubletFinder for doublet removal. Cell clusters were annotated by comparison to public datasets using SingleR. Statistical significance was determined using two-tailed Student's t-test and log-rank test. Western blotting and immunohistochemistry were performed to validate protein and tissue expression. Chemokine expression was measured via PCR analysis of lung homogenates.

Key Results
Loss of PD-L1 did not alter primary tumor growth in 4T1 or CT26 models. Knocking out PD-L1 significantly decreased lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent manner. Increased CD3+ T cell infiltration was observed in lungs of PD-L1 KO mice. PD-L1 loss did not affect initial tumor cell colonization efficiency in the lung. tPD-L1 requires a functioning adaptive immune system to promote lung metastasis. Single-cell RNA-seq revealed transcriptional changes specifically in myeloid cells. Myeloid cells showed enhanced antigen presentation machinery upon PD-L1 loss. PD-L1 engagement with mPD-1 suppressed STAT1 phosphorylation in myeloid cells. Depletion of myeloid cells diminished the metastatic advantage of PD-L1 expressing tumors. Human patient response to PD-1 blockade correlated with IFN-I response in myeloid cells.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The study uncouples the role of PD-L1 at the metastatic site from the primary tumor. Tumor PD-L1 binds to myeloid PD-1 to create an immunologically cold microenvironment. Type I interferon signaling is essential for myeloid cell function in CTL recruitment. The tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis controls CTL tumor infiltration. This mechanism explains why some tumors are resistant to PD-1 blockade in primary sites. The findings suggest that enhancing IFN-I signaling could overcome adaptive resistance. The axis underlies the efficacy of ICB in the neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study exclusively analyzed lung metastases, which may have a unique microenvironment. Conflicting findings exist regarding the necessity of tPD-L1 for response in primary tumors. The study relies on murine models which may not perfectly recapitulate human complexity. The specific contribution of other cell types besides myeloid cells to this axis is not fully explored.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I axis controlling lung metastasis. 2. The strongest evidence is the significant reduction in metastasis upon myeloid cell depletion. 3. The future path involves targeting this axis to improve immunotherapy for metastatic disease.
